projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Harry May was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran, Harry L. May, known to his friends as Pete. He served in the U.S. Army with the 143rd AAA Gun Battalion, Battery C. He served in the European theatre and his highest rank was PFC. I'm Tom Swope, and this interview was recorded in the lobby of a hotel near Columbus, Ohio, at the reunion of the 143rd AAA Battalion on July 20th, 2003. Pete was 78 at the time of this recording. When did you go into the service?

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: When I was very young. I was -- about one month after I was 18 years of age. I was very young, very small, only weighed 117 pounds, didn't even finish high school.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Drafted?

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Drafted. And I finished my high school here about two years ago. The government gave everybody their GED test, and now I have graduated from high school at the age of 56 or something like that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So what year was that when you went in?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What year did you go in then? Let me do the math here.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: July 26th.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: July 26th of '43 or '44?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: '43. So where did you train?

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: In Camp Haan, California. In the desert.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any interesting stories you can tell me from that?

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Yes. Made a lot of good friends through being in the service. And lots of times we did things that we didn't really want to, like digging fox holes and being --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: And latrine trenches.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Latrine trenches, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Latrine trenches.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Do you know what that is?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: And we did a lot of things. I know that -- a couple things I could remember, taking a 25-mile hike, 25-mile hike, and it was very, very hard and hard on you, and when we got finished, I wasn't one that rode the meat wagon. Some of them got on the meat wagon and didn't have to finish the 25 miles. But I did finish. And that very night I had to cut wood for the officers to keep them warm, and I wasn't very happy. After 25 miles I was very tired and wasn't very happy. And I can say this much: I used some words that I probably shouldn't have.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: There wasn't many of us that finished it either.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you get along with your officers overall though?

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Yes. We got along good with the officers, wouldn't you say, Joe? We had good officers, good officers, and they were good to us and they looked out for us.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Anything else from your training that comes to mind?

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Probably lots of things but it's been 50 years, you know what I mean.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: What about losing your pants?

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: One of my buddies took my pants one night and went into town, and he got rolled and robbed; and when I got my pants back, why they look like they'd been through the shredder. And I lost a wristwatch out of the pocket of my pants that night.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Your watch pocket.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Never did get it back. I lost my wallet one time when I was -- when we was on maneuvers. I lost my wallet one time, and I got it back. It was sent to my hometown where I lived with no name because of the fact I would assume the people thought that I might -- they might have taken the money out, but I had no money in it. I lost it in a poker game. So I'd like to know who they were, but I could never thank them for sending my wallet back. They probably, like I say, assumed that I figured they might have taken the money, but they didn't have any money to take.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So when did you head overseas?

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Well, when did we go overseas? Does anybody remember?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's when you disembarked, headed overseas?

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Yes. And we went to England, and that's where I first run into buzz bombs.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you have close calls with those?

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Well, we had a few close calls, but what was scary about them was you didn't know when they were gonna shut off because when they ran out of fuel that's when they come down. So as long as you could hear them, you were lucky. They would go past you. But when they run out of fuel, they was headed down. And, yes -- and I remember sleeping out in the cold, cold winter with about three or four inches of snow on me when I woke up the next morning outside because I was afraid to go in the building to sleep of any kind or a tent because of the buzz bombs. That scared me. I was afraid. Anybody wasn't afraid must have been something wrong with them. So I remember that. And you're not supposed to tell stories on yourself, but I remember I had 13 blankets in my sleeping bag. Where did I get them? Well, there's only one way to get them. You only was issued two.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: That's the ones I'm missing.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: So my other 11 I obtained somewhere, maybe on the old saying of five-finger discount. But somebody helped their self to some of my 13 blankets. I remember that. And I remember a time when we were living in tents and we went to -- remember we raided the food truck?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: We raided the food truck and we got -- had bacon in cans, chicken in cans, different things. And we would --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: We weren't hungry.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Weren't hungry. We weren't hungry. We got them illegal. So they found out they was missing, so they turned an inspection on us. So we took them out and buried them in the snow, didn't we, Joe? Then after the inspection was over we could go out and dig them up, bring them in, and eat them. It was -- it was a matter of taking care of yourself, I guess, whether it was legal or illegal or whether it was good or bad. We got through it. And army life wasn't real bad.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you get along with the British people over there?

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Yes. What little time we was there. I remember the English soldiers used to say, Give her a go, Yank. She's 18. So you can see I've been around. And that's where you first got into fish and chips. Wasn't that what they had in England? Fish and chips.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Yep.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Of course, going over on the ship I remember, too, we had Hershey bars and raw potatoes because they served us mutton. We had mutton, mutton for breakfast, mutton for dinner, mutton for super; and I ate a lot of Hershey bars and raw potatoes.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Remember that ship came from South America bringing mutton back to England.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: And the ship that we went over on was called the Highland Brigade. It's at the bottom of the sea now somewhere. They did sink it, not while we was on.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Long after, right?

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you went over to France in late August, right, of '44?

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: And we weren't allowed to whistle on deck.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Bad luck?

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: On the English ship it's bad luck. You were not allowed to whistle on deck.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Boy.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Yes. And what do you think I got duty in going overseas? I got duty just -- I don't know, just to give us something to do, they sent me right up in the front in the bow, is it, the front?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah, I guess.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: And all I could -- I got sick as a dog because all I could see was the horizon and up and down, up and down, until it wasn't long till everything was up. So I remember that, yes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was your duty up there?

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Just to watch, observation, to see if you could see anything. There was nothing -- to see if you could see anything. You know, I wouldn't know what I was seeing if I did see a ship, whether it was enemy or not.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: We were looking for subs.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Yeah. Well, or something. I don't know. There wasn't much to see anyhow but water, water, water. So I remember that.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Fourteen days to get across it.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Fourteen.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Fourteen? I heard anywhere from 14 to 17.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Coming back it took 27 days. I think Columbus came over faster than I did.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: And I remember on the way home I had one of the hardest jobs I ever had in my life when I was in the army. The hardest job was they kept calling my name to report, and I just ignored it. But they kept on calling my name, calling my name. So finally somebody said, You better go and find out. Well, the job was to call everybody's name on that deck so they could get off according to the schedule. In other words, there was number one, number two, whoever was on the deck. And I had to call their name. Some names are almost impossible to pronounce, even those you could spell them, you know, in front of you. They're hard to pronounce. And that was one of the hardest jobs I ever tackled when I was in the army. You know, you got them ski's and everything like that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Names are hard to pronounce. So I remember that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So when you went to France you landed on Utah Beach, correct?

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember your first action in -- was your first action in France then?

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: I believe so, yes.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: We went to Paris. From there we went to St-Denis.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Set up outside of Paris?

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Right outside of Paris. And it's called St-Denis, France. And that was -- I got there -- I remember getting to drink something that I never drank before. I thought I was going to die. It was called calvados. You remember it?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: And cognac.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Oh, it was tough. That was tough. It was as thick as syrup, and I'm telling you it makes you sick, it did me. Oh, was I sick. I was too sick to die. It was called calvados. But we drank a lot of cognac. At that time, cognac was measured in stars, wasn't it? Cognac measured in stars, right? And I forget what we had. I think three- or four-star cognac we drank there.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: The more stars you had --

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: The better it was. Yeah. Yep.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I was going to ask you what you did to pass your time, but I think you just told me.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: What did we do to pass the time?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Just movin.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: No. We -- we had -- we had things to do. We would practice on our guns, didn't we? I was on a 90 millimeter gun and --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was your job with the battery?

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Loader. Is that what they called them?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Ammunition loader.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Ammunition loader. That was getting the ammunition ready to throw into the breech of the gun and shoot it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Just so we mention it, this is the 143rd --

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: -- AAA --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- Battalion, Battery --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Yes. The best battery.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: The best battery.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: And probably some of the best officers. I didn't know all the officers. Yep.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you have much problem with the German Luftwaffe at that point?

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Well, that's about all they had. They had very little --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: They had almost no aircraft.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: They had a few planes but not very many. That was one -- we had to -- I remember one time I was in Belgium or someplace, maybe it was France, I'm not sure, but I was sent out. And we would -- was sent out to watch for enemy planes and was up on the hillside and sat there and watched the planes to see if any planes come. And that was one of the jobs kind of on the outer edge to watch for airplanes. Just two people, me and another person. And we stayed out there and we was -- we stayed in a gendarmerie. Do you know what a gendarmerie is?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: That is a French police. French police. We stayed in their place at night. I was out there for probably a week or so.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you have much contact with the French people when you were there?

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Oh, yes, sure.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What were they like?

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: They were good. I liked the French people, French women. They were nice. I was young. I had to chase the women, yes. I had my share of chasing the women. I enjoyed it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So how long were you set up near Paris then?

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: How long was we?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Approximately.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: We was there until Thanksgiving. We moved -- we moved to the other location in France either the day before and had our Thanksgiving dinner. We were over there about four or five days.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So I think you moved to what? Versailles, is that right?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right around Thanksgiving?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: I remember another incident in St-Denis. I run into this girl and got to know her. Her brother came around. And I didn't smoke. So I said, Boy, I sure could go for some chicken. And they said, well, they would get me a chicken. And I said, I'll give so many cigarettes for a chicken. I said I could eat a whole chicken myself. So they got the chicken, and they invited me over for chicken dinner, and they gave -- shoved the whole thing in front of me and wanted me to eat the whole thing because I had said that. That was just an expression I used, I could eat a whole chicken, but they thought I really meant it, that I would eat the whole chicken. So, no, I shared it with them and I enjoyed the evening. It was only about a five-minute walk from where we was in St-Denis. They lived in a condominium building of some kind, you know. It was nice. I enjoyed that. I enjoyed different parts. There were some bad parts.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah?

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any of those you want to share?

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: I don't know any I need to share. Do you know anything?

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: No. I don't remember that. No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So how long were you in Versailles then?

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Here's the guy that knows more about --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah. We'll get to you. In Versailles you moved into position for the Battle of the Bulge. You moved into Belgium, right?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: We went to Belgium.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Battle of the Bulge, yes. We were in the Battle of the Bulge. And there's another time I was scared to death because what planes there was they would strafe at us, wouldn't they? They'd come in on the run and they'd try to strafe you if you was on the ground, and that was scary. Who knows where shells are coming -- or bullets are coming from? You know. You don't know whether you're gonna get it in the back or back of your head or leg or where else. So that was bad. And that only lasted, what? How long was we there? Four or five days, wasn't it?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Not very long.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Not very long with the Battle of the Bulge.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: The Battle of the Bulge --

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Well, what I meant when we was under fire mostly, you know, because from then I think we went to anny tank, didn't we?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were you with the group that was at the station at Stumont?

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: No, I wasn't with you, was I, Joe? Was I there with you?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Was I?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Oh, God.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Remember, our gun -- our gun was the only one that was saved out of the four.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I heard that.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Okay. Yeah. I was on the same gun as he was. I must have been there, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you were involved in the incident where they were shooting at the tank, right?

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Oh, yes, yes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What do you remember about that?

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Oh, God. Why you asking me that? That's been 50 some years ago.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I got one of the other guys talking about it, and I just wanted to know what you remembered.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Nothing special.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You weren't the one that scored the lucky hit that hit the barrel of the tank.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: How would you know?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well, you were involved.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: How would you know if you was one of them or not?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You were involved.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: I was just one of so many on a gun tour, right?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well, you were all involved.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Anything else you remember from that, though, from those opening days of the Battle of the Bulge?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: I remember one thing. Remember when we were going up -- there was a two-lane road. There was two lanes. The road was loaded with trucks with Americans that were retreating and we're going forward. Remember that?

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: We said, What the hell are we going forward for?

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Goin the wrong way.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Aren't you supposed to be behind them?

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: We're goin the wrong way. Everybody else was retreating and we're goin the wrong way. I don't know. You know, after 50 years you kind of -- you kind of forget a few things.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Anything you might have said today at the reunion that you thought about you want to talk about?

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: No, I don't think so.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When you think about that, when you start thinking about it at the reunion or whatever, does one vivid memory come to mind about World War II?

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: No, not necessarily.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Nothing jumps out.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Nothing jumps out.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were you in the army of occupation then after?

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Afterwards?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-hum.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: We were collecting guns remember?

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: We was -- we got discharged in -- was it Belgium we got discharged or where was we at?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Well, I wasn't with you people, remember? I ended up in the hospital.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Well, I was in the hospital once.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wounded?

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Let's hear about that.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: You don't want to hear about that.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Woman wounded.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: That was an accident.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: With a woman? What?

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: No. It was an accident.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: It was an accident. Okay.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Oh, yeah. You gotta tell them that.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: One of my own buddies accidentally shot me.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How did that happen?

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: I don't know. All I know --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: He was cleaning a .22 rifle that he found.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-hum.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: He had the round in the chamber. He didn't know how to take it out. He pulled the trigger and he was sittin in front of him.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: I was sittin there, and it went in my -- it's in my ankle, in the ankle bone, and it's been there; and the government gives me a nice little check every month. And it's amounted to quite a few thousand dollars.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's right. And do you send him a Christmas card every year?

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Somebody said he died.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Who?

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: George Walsh died. That's what they say, he died. I'd like to see him. I don't hold nothing against him. You know. It's one of them things.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: It was an accident.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Accidents will happen.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Remember, I was laying on my bed, and you were sitting on my quilt closet. He could have killed either one of us.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: No sweat.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Anything else?

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: No. I can't think of anything else. I probably could think of a hundred things if somebody could tell me, you know, or refreshed my memory, but --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's always the case. As soon as we're done, tomorrow you'll think of something.

sp.speaker: Harry May
sp.p: Probably.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That happens all the time.
